name: Nervous system
description: The brain, spinal cord and nerves: nerve cells and signals, the lobes and main areas of the cortex, the brainstem and cerebellum, the deep structures, the ventricles and coverings, the twelve cranial nerves, the spinal cord and nerves, and the autonomic system. Picture questions show the brain, drawn see-through, with one part highlighted to name.

source.name: Written for Study Buddy. Pictures rendered from BodyParts3D (© The Database Center for Life Science, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP).

questions.prompt: Which two parts make up the central nervous system?
answers: The brain and the spinal cord
questions.explanation: Everything outside them (the cranial and spinal nerves and the ganglia) is the peripheral nervous system.

questions.prompt: What is the basic signalling cell of the nervous system called?
questions.explanation: The brain has about 86 billion of them.

questions.prompt: Which part of a neuron receives incoming signals from other cells?
questions.explanation: Short, branching and usually many. The cell body (soma) holds the nucleus.

questions.prompt: Which part of a neuron carries the signal away from the cell body?
questions.explanation: One long fibre per neuron, which can reach a metre or more, as in the nerves to your foot.

questions.prompt: What fatty insulating layer wrapped around many axons speeds up the signal?
questions.explanation: In peripheral nerves it is made by Schwann cells; in the brain and cord by oligodendrocytes.

questions.prompt: What are the gaps in the myelin sheath, where the signal is boosted, called?
questions.explanation: The impulse jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction), which is much faster than travelling along bare axon.

questions.prompt: Which disease attacks the myelin of the central nervous system, slowing or blocking nerve signals?
questions.explanation: Lesions (plaques) form in the white matter, so signals along the affected fibres slow or fail.

questions.prompt: Which cells make the myelin of peripheral nerves?
questions.explanation: One Schwann cell wraps one stretch of one axon; an oligodendrocyte in the CNS wraps several.

questions.prompt: Which glial cells make myelin in the brain and spinal cord?
Which star-shaped glial cells support neurons and help form the blood–brain barrier?
questions.explanation: They also tidy up neurotransmitters and feed neurons.

questions.prompt: Which glial cells are the immune cells of the central nervous system?
questions.explanation: They clear away debris and damaged cells.

questions.prompt: Which glial cells line the ventricles and make cerebrospinal fluid circulate?
About what is the resting membrane potential of a neuron?
questions.explanation: The inside of the cell is negative compared with the outside, because of potassium leak channels and the sodium–potassium pump.

questions.prompt: Which ions rush into a neuron to start the rising phase of an action potential?
questions.explanation: Voltage-gated sodium channels open once the threshold is reached; potassium leaving the cell then brings the voltage back down.

questions.prompt: What does 'all or none' mean for an action potential?
answers: It either fires fully or not at all
Once the threshold is reached it always has the same size
wrong: Its size grows with the stimulus
It always travels at the same speed in every axon
It fires only at the synapse
questions.explanation: A stronger stimulus makes the neuron fire more often, not harder.

questions.prompt: What is the junction where one neuron signals to another cell called?
questions.explanation: Most are chemical: the signal crosses a narrow gap (the synaptic cleft) as a neurotransmitter.

questions.prompt: Where are neurotransmitters stored in the axon terminal before release?
questions.explanation: Calcium entering the terminal makes the vesicles fuse with the membrane and empty into the cleft.

questions.prompt: Which amino acid is the main excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain?
questions.explanation: GABA is the main inhibitory one in the brain; glycine does that in the spinal cord.

questions.prompt: Which neurotransmitter is the main inhibitory one in the brain?
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines and alcohol calm the brain partly by boosting GABA's effect.

questions.prompt: Which neurotransmitter is lost in Parkinson's disease because cells of the substantia nigra die?
questions.explanation: It is also central to reward and motivation.

questions.prompt: Which neurotransmitter do SSRI antidepressants raise?
questions.explanation: SSRI means selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor: it stops the transmitter being taken back up.

questions.prompt: Which neurotransmitter do motor neurons release onto skeletal muscle?
questions.explanation: Also the transmitter of the parasympathetic system. Alzheimer's disease damages acetylcholine-using neurons.

questions.prompt: What is grey matter mostly made of?
questions.explanation: White matter is mostly myelinated axons: the white is the fatty myelin.

questions.prompt: What is the largest part of the human brain called?
questions.explanation: Two hemispheres joined by the corpus callosum, covered by the folded cortex.

figure.alt: The brain from the left
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: What are the ridges and the grooves of the folded cerebral cortex called?
questions.explanation: Folding packs about 2,500 cm² of cortex into the skull. The deepest grooves are fissures.

questions.prompt: What are the four lobes of each cerebral hemisphere?
questions.explanation: Named after the skull bones over them. The insula, tucked deep in the lateral sulcus, is sometimes counted as a fifth.

questions.prompt: Which groove separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe?
questions.explanation: The motor gyrus lies in front of it and the sensory gyrus behind it.

questions.prompt: Which deep groove separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes?
Which deep groove separates the two cerebral hemispheres?
questions.explanation: The falx cerebri, a fold of dura, lies in it.

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The strip of frontal lobe just in front of the central sulcus.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which area of the cortex sends the commands for voluntary movement?
questions.explanation: It is laid out as a map of the body (the motor homunculus), with the hands and face taking up most of it.

figure.alt: The brain with the primary motor cortex in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The strip of parietal lobe just behind the central sulcus.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which area of the cortex receives touch, pressure and pain from the body?
questions.explanation: Like the motor cortex, it is a map of the body, and the lips and fingertips take up the most room.

figure.alt: The brain with the primary somatosensory cortex in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: What is the distorted body map drawn over the motor and sensory cortex called?
questions.explanation: Body parts with fine control or fine touch (hands, lips, tongue) get the most cortex.

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The top ridge of the frontal lobe, running along the edge of the longitudinal fissure. Seen here from above.

figure.alt: The brain from above, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: Part of the prefrontal cortex, which plans, decides and holds things in mind.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the frontal lobe is the seat of planning, decision-making and self-control?
questions.explanation: It matures last, into the mid-twenties. Damage can change personality, as in the famous case of Phineas Gage.

figure.alt: The brain with part of the prefrontal cortex in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Damage to which area of the left frontal lobe leaves a person understanding speech but unable to produce fluent words?
questions.explanation: Broca's aphasia: speech comes slowly and effortfully, but the meaning is there. It lies in the inferior frontal gyrus.

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: Part of the parietal lobe, curving over the end of the lateral sulcus. It helps with language and with touch.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: Part of the parietal lobe, curving over the end of the superior temporal sulcus. It helps with reading and with maths.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The top ridge of the temporal lobe, with the auditory cortex on its upper surface.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which lobe holds the primary auditory cortex?
questions.explanation: Tucked in the superior temporal gyrus, deep in the lateral sulcus.

figure.alt: The brain with the superior temporal gyrus in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: Wernicke's area, in the left hemisphere for most people, makes sense of spoken and written words.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Damage to Wernicke's area leaves speech fluent but empty of sense. What is it called?
questions.explanation: The words flow but are jumbled, and the person doesn't follow what is said.

figure.alt: The brain with Wernicke's area in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The middle ridge of the temporal lobe, involved in recognising words and faces.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The lowest ridge on the side of the temporal lobe, seen here from below and the side. It helps with recognising objects.

figure.alt: The brain from below, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The back of the brain, where vision is processed.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which lobe holds the primary visual cortex?
questions.explanation: A stroke here can blind one side of the visual field in both eyes (homonymous hemianopia) without any damage to the eyes.

figure.alt: The brain with the occipital lobe in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: Folded deep inside the lateral sulcus (the cortex that covers it is drawn see-through). It handles taste, pain and gut feelings.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: Wraps over the corpus callosum on the inner face of each hemisphere. It is part of the limbic system. Seen here from the inner face.

figure.alt: The middle of the brain, from the right, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which lobe combines touch and position into a sense of where your body and the things around you are?
questions.explanation: Damage to the right parietal lobe can lead to neglect of the left side of space.

questions.prompt: Which lobe holds the hippocampus, central to forming new memories?
In most people, which hemisphere is dominant for language?
questions.explanation: True for nearly all right-handed people and most left-handed ones.

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The great band of about 200 million fibres joining the two hemispheres. Seen here from the middle of the brain.

figure.alt: The middle of the brain, from the right, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: What is cut in 'split-brain' surgery, once used for severe epilepsy?
questions.explanation: The two hemispheres then work with little exchange of information.

figure.alt: The brain with the corpus callosum in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The stalk joining the brain to the spinal cord, made of the midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: From top to bottom, what are the three parts of the brainstem?
questions.explanation: Ten of the twelve cranial nerves leave from it. It also carries every signal between brain and body.

figure.alt: The brain with the brainstem in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The top of the brainstem. Its back holds the colliculi; its front holds the cerebral peduncles.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which two cranial nerves leave from the midbrain?
questions.explanation: Both move the eyes.

figure.alt: The brain with the midbrain in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The bulge in the middle of the brainstem. 'Pons' is Latin for bridge, because its fibres connect the two halves of the cerebellum.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerves leave from the pons?
questions.explanation: The trigeminal, abducens, facial and vestibulocochlear nerves. The pons also helps to control breathing.

figure.alt: The brain with the pons in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The lowest part of the brainstem, continuous with the spinal cord.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brainstem holds the control centres for heart rate, breathing and blood pressure?
questions.explanation: Damage here is often fatal. The medulla also coordinates vomiting, coughing and swallowing.

figure.alt: The brain with the medulla oblongata in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Where do most motor fibres from the cortex cross to the other side on their way down?
answers: In the medulla (the decussation of the pyramids)
questions.explanation: This is why the left side of the brain controls the right side of the body.

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The 'little brain' at the back and bottom of the skull, tucked under the occipital lobe.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain coordinates movement, balance and posture without our noticing?
questions.explanation: It holds more than half of the brain's neurons. Damage causes unsteady movement (ataxia) and tremor on reaching.

figure.alt: The brain with the cerebellum in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: A drunk person staggers and cannot touch a finger to their nose accurately. Which part of the brain is the alcohol hitting hardest?
questions.explanation: Cerebellar signs: staggering, slurred speech and intention tremor.

questions.prompt: Which network of neurons running up the brainstem keeps the brain awake and alert?
questions.explanation: General anaesthetics work partly by quietening it.

questions.prompt: Which structures are highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: Four small bumps on the back of the midbrain. The upper pair handle visual reflexes and the lower pair auditory ones. Seen here from behind and above.

figure.alt: The brain from behind, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which pair of bumps on the back of the midbrain turns the eyes and head towards a sudden movement?
questions.explanation: The inferior colliculi are for sound: a relay on the way to the auditory cortex.

figure.alt: The brain with the colliculi in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: Two egg-shaped masses either side of the third ventricle, in the middle of the brain.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which structure is the main relay station for sensory signals on their way to the cortex?
questions.explanation: Every sense except smell goes through it.

figure.alt: The brain with the thalamus in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: A small but crucial region below the thalamus, at the base of the brain, with the mammillary bodies at its back.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which small structure controls body temperature, thirst, hunger, and links the nervous system to the endocrine system?
questions.explanation: It makes the hormones released by the posterior pituitary and the releasing hormones that control the anterior pituitary.

figure.alt: The brain with the hypothalamus in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: A tiny pine-cone-shaped gland at the back of the third ventricle.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which hormone, made by the pineal gland in the dark, helps set the sleep cycle?

figure.alt: The brain with the pineal body in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: A pea-sized gland hanging from the hypothalamus, sitting in the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone. Seen here from the left.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which gland is called the 'master gland' because its hormones control other glands?
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus, in turn, controls the pituitary.

figure.alt: The brain with the pituitary gland in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which structure is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: A curved fold of cortex in the inside of the temporal lobe, shaped like a seahorse (hippocampus in Greek).

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which structure is essential for turning short-term memories into long-term ones?
questions.explanation: Patient H.M. had both hippocampi removed in 1953 and could no longer form new memories. It is among the first places damaged in Alzheimer's disease.

figure.alt: The brain with the hippocampus in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which structure is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: An almond-shaped (amygdala in Greek) cluster of nuclei at the front of the temporal lobe, next to the hippocampus.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which almond-shaped structure is central to fear and to attaching emotion to memories?

figure.alt: The brain with the amygdala in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which group of structures, including the hippocampus, amygdala and cingulate gyrus, deals with emotion and memory?
questions.explanation: Limbus is Latin for border: it rings the brainstem.

questions.prompt: Which group of structures is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: Deep clusters of grey matter: the caudate nucleus, the putamen and the globus pallidus (with the substantia nigra and subthalamic nucleus).

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which group of deep nuclei helps start and smooth voluntary movements, and is damaged in Parkinson's and Huntington's diseases?

figure.alt: The brain with the basal ganglia in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The tail-shaped (caudate means having a tail) nucleus arching round the lateral ventricle.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The outer, rounded part of the lentiform nucleus, next to the insula.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The pale inner part of the lentiform nucleus, inside the putamen.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which two nuclei together are called the striatum?
questions.explanation: Bands of white matter run through them, giving a striped (striated) look.

questions.prompt: In Parkinson's disease, cells die in which midbrain nucleus that sends dopamine to the striatum?
questions.explanation: Nigra means black: its cells hold dark melanin. The result is tremor at rest, slow movement and stiffness.

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: A band of white matter between the thalamus and the basal ganglia, through which nearly all fibres to and from the cortex pass.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: A small stroke in which narrow band of white matter can paralyse the whole opposite side of the body?
questions.explanation: All the motor fibres are packed tightly there.

figure.alt: The brain with the internal capsule in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: An arched bundle of fibres carrying signals from the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies and hypothalamus. Seen here from the middle of the brain.

figure.alt: The middle of the brain, from the right, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: Two small round bumps (mammillary means nipple-like) at the back of the hypothalamus, part of the memory circuit.

figure.alt: The middle of the brain, from the right, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which structures are highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: Two knee-shaped (geniculate) bumps on the underside of each thalamus: the lateral one relays vision and the medial one hearing.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which relay in the thalamus passes signals from the optic tract to the visual cortex?
questions.explanation: The medial geniculate relays hearing.

figure.alt: The brain with the geniculate bodies in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The X-shaped crossing of the two optic nerves, just in front of the pituitary gland. Seen here from below.

figure.alt: The brain from below, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: What crosses to the opposite side at the optic chiasm?
answers: Fibres from the inner (nasal) half of each retina
The nasal half of each retina
wrong: Fibres from the outer half of each retina
questions.explanation: That way each hemisphere sees the opposite half of the visual field with both eyes.

figure.alt: The brain from below with the optic chiasm in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: A pituitary tumour pressing upwards on the optic chiasm causes loss of which part of vision?
answers: The outer halves of both visual fields
wrong: The left half of both visual fields
The upper half of both visual fields
questions.explanation: Called bitemporal hemianopia: the crossing fibres from the inner halves of the retinas are squeezed first.

questions.prompt: Which structures are highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: From the retina to the chiasm is the optic nerve; from the chiasm to the thalamus is the optic tract. Seen here from below.

figure.alt: The brain from below, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which system is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: Four fluid-filled chambers joined together by narrow channels, deep in the brain.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: How many ventricles are in the brain?
questions.explanation: Two lateral ventricles, the third ventricle and the fourth ventricle.

figure.alt: The brain with the ventricles in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The two large C-shaped chambers, one in each hemisphere.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The narrow slit between the two halves of the thalamus.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: In front of the cerebellum and behind the pons and medulla.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The thin channel through the midbrain, joining the third ventricle to the fourth.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: In what order does cerebrospinal fluid flow through the ventricles?
questions.explanation: From the fourth ventricle it leaves through small openings into the subarachnoid space around the brain, and also runs down the central canal of the spinal cord.

questions.prompt: Which structure is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: Tufts of blood vessels lining the ventricles.

figure.alt: The brain from the left, with one part in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Where is cerebrospinal fluid mostly made?
questions.explanation: About 500 mL is made each day, but only about 150 mL is present at a time, because it is constantly reabsorbed.

figure.alt: The brain with the choroid plexus in red
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Through which structures is cerebrospinal fluid absorbed back into the blood?
questions.explanation: They poke into the superior sagittal venous sinus.

questions.prompt: What is it called when cerebrospinal fluid builds up in the ventricles, as when the aqueduct is blocked?
questions.explanation: In babies the head enlarges. A shunt drains the extra fluid.

questions.prompt: From outside to inside, what are the three meninges around the brain?
answers: Dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater
wrong: Pia mater, arachnoid mater, dura mater
Arachnoid mater, dura mater, pia mater
Dura mater, pia mater, arachnoid mater
questions.explanation: Dura (tough mother), arachnoid (spider-web-like) and pia (gentle mother). The cerebrospinal fluid is in the space between the last two, the subarachnoid space.

questions.prompt: What is the inflammation of the meninges, usually from infection, called?
questions.explanation: Typical signs are fever, headache and a stiff neck.

questions.prompt: A skull fracture that tears the middle meningeal artery causes bleeding into which space?
answers: Between the skull and the dura mater
questions.explanation: An epidural haematoma. Subdural bleeding tears the bridging veins instead, and subarachnoid bleeding is usually from a ruptured aneurysm.

questions.prompt: What keeps many blood-borne substances from entering the brain tissue?
questions.explanation: Tight junctions between the capillary cells, with support from astrocytes. It blocks many drugs, which is a problem for treating brain tumours.

questions.prompt: What is the ring of arteries at the base of the brain, joining the carotid and basilar supplies, called?
questions.explanation: If one artery is blocked the others can often make up the supply.

questions.prompt: How many pairs of cranial nerves are there?
questions.explanation: Named and numbered in Roman numerals from front to back.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve carries the sense of smell?
questions.explanation: Its fibres pass through the holes of the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve carries vision?
questions.explanation: It is really a tract of the brain, wrapped in meninges, which is why damage doesn't regrow.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve moves most of the muscles that move the eye, lifts the eyelid and constricts the pupil?
questions.explanation: When it fails the eye points down and out, the lid droops and the pupil is large.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve supplies the superior oblique muscle of the eye?
questions.explanation: The only cranial nerve to leave from the back of the brainstem. Its muscle works through a pulley (trochlea).

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve carries feeling from the face and moves the chewing muscles?
questions.explanation: Three branches (ophthalmic, maxillary and mandibular) give it its name.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve supplies the lateral rectus muscle, turning the eye outward?
questions.explanation: Abducens abducts the eye. Paralysis makes the eye drift inward and causes double vision.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve moves the muscles of facial expression and carries taste from the front of the tongue?
questions.explanation: In Bell's palsy the nerve is inflamed and one side of the face droops.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve carries hearing and balance from the inner ear?
questions.explanation: The cochlear part is for hearing and the vestibular part for balance.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve carries taste from the back of the tongue and supplies the muscle that lifts the pharynx in swallowing?
questions.explanation: Glosso- is tongue, pharyngeal is throat. It also senses blood pressure at the carotid sinus.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve runs from the brainstem all the way to the abdomen, slowing the heart and speeding up digestion?
questions.explanation: Vagus means wanderer. It carries most of the parasympathetic outflow.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve supplies the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid?
questions.explanation: Testing a shrug and turning the head against resistance checks it.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve moves the tongue?
questions.explanation: Hypo- (under) glossal (tongue). When it fails, the tongue sticks out to the damaged side.

questions.prompt: Which three cranial nerves move the eyeball?
answers: Cranial nerves III, IV and VI
questions.explanation: Memory aid for the muscles: LR6 SO4 and the rest 3. Lateral rectus is supplied by VI, superior oblique by IV and the others by III.

questions.prompt: In order, I to XII, what are the cranial nerves?
answers: Olfactory, optic, oculomotor, trochlear, trigeminal, abducens, facial, vestibulocochlear, glossopharyngeal, vagus, accessory, hypoglossal
wrong: Optic, olfactory, oculomotor, trochlear, trigeminal, abducens, facial, vestibulocochlear, glossopharyngeal, vagus, accessory, hypoglossal
Olfactory, optic, trochlear, oculomotor, trigeminal, abducens, facial, vestibulocochlear, glossopharyngeal, vagus, accessory, hypoglossal
Olfactory, optic, oculomotor, trochlear, trigeminal, facial, abducens, vestibulocochlear, glossopharyngeal, vagus, accessory, hypoglossal
questions.explanation: "Oh, Oh, Oh, To Touch And Feel Very Good Velvet, Such Heaven": the first letters give O O O T T A F V G V A H.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerves carry only sensory signals (the special senses)?
answers: Cranial nerves I, II and VIII
questions.explanation: "Some say marry money, but my brother says big brains matter more": S = sensory, M = motor, B = both: S S M M B M M B B B M M for I to XII.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerves leave from the medulla?
questions.explanation: The last four.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve is affected in Bell's palsy?
questions.explanation: The forehead droops too, unlike in a stroke: the part of the face above the eyes is supplied from both hemispheres.

questions.prompt: Sudden stabbing pain in one side of the face, set off by a light touch or chewing, comes from which nerve?
questions.explanation: Trigeminal neuralgia, often from a blood vessel pressing on the nerve root.

questions.prompt: In an adult, the spinal cord ends at about which vertebra?
questions.explanation: The conus medullaris. Below it, the nerve roots hang down like a horse's tail (the cauda equina). A lumbar puncture is done below this, between L3 and L4 or L4 and L5.

questions.prompt: What are the bundle of nerve roots below the end of the spinal cord called?
questions.explanation: Latin for horse's tail. Compression of it is a surgical emergency: numbness between the legs and loss of bladder control.

questions.prompt: How many pairs of spinal nerves are there?
questions.explanation: Eight cervical, 12 thoracic, five lumbar, five sacral and one coccygeal.

questions.prompt: There are seven cervical vertebrae. How many pairs of cervical spinal nerves are there?
questions.explanation: C1 leaves above the atlas and C8 below the C7 vertebra; below that, each nerve leaves below its vertebra.

questions.prompt: Which root of a spinal nerve carries sensory signals into the cord?
wrong: Neither: sensory signals go through the cauda equina
questions.explanation: Its cell bodies are in the dorsal root ganglion. The ventral root carries motor signals out.

questions.prompt: Which root of a spinal nerve carries motor signals out from the cord?
questions.explanation: The Bell–Magendie law: dorsal for sensory (in), ventral for motor (out).

questions.prompt: In cross-section, the grey matter of the spinal cord is shaped like what?
answers: A butterfly or the letter H
wrong: A horseshoe only in the neck
questions.explanation: With the white matter in tracts around it, the reverse of the brain, where grey matter is on the outside.

questions.prompt: Which tracts in the back of the spinal cord carry fine touch and the sense of limb position up to the brain?
questions.explanation: They cross in the medulla. The spinothalamic tracts, which carry pain and temperature, cross in the cord itself, within a few segments of entering.

questions.prompt: Which tract carries voluntary movement commands from the motor cortex down the spinal cord?
questions.explanation: Most of its fibres cross in the medulla's pyramids.

questions.prompt: Which tract carries pain and temperature signals up to the thalamus?
questions.explanation: Its fibres cross within a few segments of the cord, so a one-sided cord injury loses pain on the other side of the body below it.

questions.prompt: A half-cut of the spinal cord weakens one side of the body and takes pain and temperature from the other. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Motor and touch fibres cross higher up (in the medulla), pain fibres cross in the cord.

questions.prompt: What is the area of skin supplied by the sensory fibres of one spinal nerve called?
questions.explanation: A myotome is the set of muscles one spinal nerve moves.

questions.prompt: What is a network where the spinal nerves join and regroup before running to the limbs called?
questions.explanation: The main ones are the cervical, brachial, lumbar and sacral plexuses.

questions.prompt: Which plexus supplies the shoulder and the whole upper limb?
questions.explanation: Formed from the ventral rami of C5 to T1. Its roots pass between the anterior and middle scalenes.

questions.prompt: Which nerve to the diaphragm comes from C3, C4 and C5?
questions.explanation: "C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive."

questions.prompt: Which is the largest nerve in the body?
questions.explanation: It leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, below the piriformis, and splits above the knee into the tibial and common fibular nerves. Sciatica is pain along it.

questions.prompt: Compression of which nerve at the wrist causes carpal tunnel syndrome?
questions.explanation: Tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers, and weakness of the thumb.

questions.prompt: Which nerve runs behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus (the 'funny bone')?
questions.explanation: Knocking it sends a tingling to the little finger and half of the ring finger.

questions.prompt: A broken shaft of the humerus can damage which nerve, causing wrist drop?
questions.explanation: It winds round the back of the humerus in the radial groove and supplies all the extensor muscles of the arm and forearm.

questions.prompt: Which nerve winds round the neck of the fibula and, when injured, causes foot drop?
questions.explanation: It supplies the muscles that lift the foot.

questions.prompt: Which nerve supplies the quadriceps?
questions.explanation: Branches from L2 to L4. The obturator nerve supplies the adductors.

questions.prompt: What are the five parts of a reflex arc, in order?
answers: Receptor, sensory neuron, integration centre, motor neuron, effector
wrong: Receptor, motor neuron, integration centre, sensory neuron, effector
Effector, sensory neuron, integration centre, motor neuron, receptor
Receptor, sensory neuron, effector, motor neuron, integration centre
questions.explanation: Spinal reflexes act without waiting for the brain, which makes them fast.

questions.prompt: The knee-jerk reflex is a stretch reflex. What does the tap on the patellar tendon stretch?
questions.explanation: The quadriceps contracts at once, with only one synapse between the sensory and motor neurons (a monosynaptic reflex).

questions.prompt: Touching something hot makes you snatch your hand away before you feel pain. Where is this reflex integrated?
questions.explanation: The pain signal also goes up to the brain, but later.

questions.prompt: Which sensory receptor in a tendon senses tension and makes the muscle relax if it is too much?
questions.explanation: A muscle spindle senses stretch in the muscle itself.

questions.prompt: What does the autonomic nervous system control?
answers: Involuntary functions such as heart rate and digestion
Smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands
questions.explanation: It has two main parts, the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions, and a third, the enteric nervous system of the gut.

questions.prompt: Which division of the autonomic nervous system prepares the body for 'fight or flight'?
questions.explanation: Heart rate and blood pressure rise, the airways widen, the pupils dilate and digestion slows.

questions.prompt: Which division of the autonomic nervous system promotes 'rest and digest'?
questions.explanation: Heart rate falls, digestion speeds up, the pupils narrow.

questions.prompt: Sympathetic neurons leave the spinal cord from which levels?
questions.explanation: The 'thoracolumbar outflow'. The parasympathetic outflow is cranial and sacral.

questions.prompt: The parasympathetic outflow comes from which parts of the central nervous system?
questions.explanation: Cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X, and spinal nerves S2 to S4.

questions.prompt: Which neurotransmitter do all preganglionic autonomic neurons release?
questions.explanation: Postganglionic parasympathetic neurons also use ACh; most postganglionic sympathetic neurons use noradrenaline.

questions.prompt: Which neurotransmitter do most postganglionic sympathetic neurons release?
questions.explanation: A few, such as those to sweat glands, use acetylcholine.

questions.prompt: The adrenal medulla is like a sympathetic ganglion that releases hormones into the blood. Which?
What effect does stimulation of the vagus nerve have on the heart?
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine acts on the sinoatrial node. At rest the vagus keeps the heart rate below the 100 beats a minute the node would set by itself.

questions.prompt: Which division of the autonomic nervous system widens (dilates) the pupil?
questions.explanation: The parasympathetic constricts it, through the oculomotor nerve.

questions.prompt: What is the network of nerves in the wall of the gut, which can run digestion without the brain, called?
questions.explanation: It has some 500 million neurons, so it is sometimes called the 'second brain'.

questions.prompt: How many neurons are in the pathway from the central nervous system to the effector in the somatic system, and in the autonomic system?
answers: One in the somatic, two in the autonomic
wrong: Two in the somatic, one in the autonomic
questions.explanation: The autonomic pathway has a preganglionic and a postganglionic neuron, with a synapse in a ganglion between them.

tests.name: Name the part
tests.why: Twenty pictures of the brain, each with one part in red to name.

tests.name: Chapter quiz
tests.why: Thirty questions from the whole chapter, marked at the end, like an end-of-unit test.

tests.name: Recall without choices
tests.why: Type each answer from memory, starting with the ones due for review. Small typos are forgiven.
